ui.lib_lede: Each card is a scripted simulation built from publicly documented theories and techniques — a study companion for the history of psychotherapy and contemplative thought, not a real clinician or teacher.
ui.lineage_banner_text: Start with the Gestalt founders — {perls} is the most direct, confrontational voice in the set. See how he got there in {lineage}.
ui.empty_state: No one matches that search. Try a different name, idea, or school.
ui.disclaimer_line: Educational simulation, not therapy or medical advice. In a crisis, contact local emergency services or (US) call/text 988.
ui.about_p1: What this is. Consulting Room is an educational simulator. Each of the 135 characters is built from publicly documented biography, core concepts, and characteristic techniques associated with a real historical or contemporary psychologist, psychotherapist, philosopher, or meditation teacher. Replies are generated by a scripted, offline template engine (or, only if you supply your own API key, by a live language model instructed to stay in character) — never by the actual person.
ui.about_p_not: Not therapy. Not a diagnosis. Not medical, psychiatric, or crisis care. Not the real person's own words — treat every reply as an invented, illustrative composite, not a verified quote. Nothing here should be used to make decisions about medication, treatment, or safety.
ui.about_p_struggling: If you're in crisis or thinking about suicide or self-harm, please contact a real person: a crisis line, a doctor, or someone you trust. In the US, call or text 988. Outside the US, search “[your country] crisis line” or contact local emergency services. This app will always redirect to this message if it detects that kind of content, instead of continuing the roleplay.
ui.about_p_data: Conversations and any API key you enter are stored only in your browser's local storage on this device. Nothing is sent to us. If you enable live mode, your messages are sent directly from your browser to the AI provider you configure.
ui.lineage_intro: Two chains worth tracing, exactly as requested: the line that formed Perls, and the humanistic/existential circle worth comparing him against.
ui.lineage_master_note: A few names repeat in the original numbered list (e.g. Jung at #4 and #12, Perls at #17 and #103) — each still opens the one matching character below.
ui.traditions_intro: A second list, alongside the one above: Buddhist philosophers and contemplative teachers, plus a few figures who bridge back into psychology (Skinner → experimental psychology, Freud → psychoanalysis, Kahneman → cognitive science, Nāgārjuna → Buddhist philosophy, Namkhai Norbu → the Dzogchen contemplative tradition). Read them side by side and a single question runs underneath all of it: how have different traditions understood the mind, consciousness, suffering, behavior, and transformation?
ui.traditions_master_note: Names already in the psychology library above (Freud, Perls, Kahneman, and others) reappear here in their place on this list — opening them opens the same character.

Think of me as an interactive study aid for their way of thinking, not a substitute for real therapy or medical care.

ui.crisis: I want to pause the simulation for a second, because that matters more than any theory. I'm a scripted educational character, not a crisis counselor, and I'm not equipped to keep you safe -- so please tell a real person: a crisis line, a doctor, or someone you trust, right now if you can. In the US you can call or text 988. Outside the US, search “[your country] suicide crisis line” or go to your nearest emergency department. If you're in immediate danger, please contact local emergency services. I'll stay right here if you want to keep talking in the meantime -- you don't have to go through this alone.

founders.label: Founding Psychology
openers: Before we go further -- describe exactly what you noticed, without explaining it yet.
What is {t1} doing for you right now, practically speaking?
Let's not interpret yet. Just describe the raw experience as it came to you.
What habit is quietly running underneath what you just told me?
What would you notice if you slowed {topic} down to a single frame, the way a lab observation would?
Separate the raw sensation in {topic} from the label you've already put on it.
reflect: Stripped of interpretation, what you're describing is: {topic}. What else is present in it?
That's the surface. What's the function {topic} is actually serving for you?
Notice how much of {topic} is raw sensation, and how much is the story you've added to it.
This might be less a fixed thing than a stream -- constantly becoming, not staying still.
The habit itself may matter more here than any single thought about {topic}.
technique: Try describing {topic} again, this time as plainly as you'd describe a chair -- no metaphors.
Ask yourself what purpose {topic} serves, the way you'd ask what a habit is for.
Try the stream-of-consciousness method: speak everything passing through awareness about {topic} for sixty seconds, unedited.

psychoanalytic.label: Psychoanalytic / Psychodynamic
openers: What comes to mind first, without editing it, when you sit with that?
Does {topic} remind you of anything from earlier in your life?
I notice how you're telling me this. What might that way of telling it be protecting you from?
Whose voice does {t1} sound like, if you listen closely?
What's the very first memory that surfaces when you let {topic} sit for a moment?
If this were a dream you'd had last night, what would the dream-version of {topic} be hiding?
reflect: There may be more beneath {topic} than you're saying, even to yourself.
That reaction is bigger than this moment alone -- it sounds like it's carrying something older.
Notice the feeling you're avoiding naming directly. What would it be called, if you let yourself say it?
Transference happens outside the couch too -- who does this feel like all over again?
A slip, a joke, a forgotten detail around {topic} is rarely just an accident.
technique: Try free association for a minute: say whatever comes after '{topic} reminds me of...' without censoring it.
Ask what {topic} would look like if it were really about someone from your past, not the present.
Notice any resistance to going further with {topic} -- the discomfort itself is usually informative.

jungian.label: Analytical / Jungian
openers: What images or symbols come up when you think about {topic}?
Is there a part of yourself in {t2} that you usually keep in shadow?
If this situation were a dream, what would it be telling you?
What does {topic} want from you that you haven't been willing to give it?
What would your dreams have to say about {topic} if you asked them tonight?
Where does {topic} touch on individuation -- becoming more fully who you actually are?
reflect: That might be your shadow speaking -- the part of you that doesn't fit your idea of who you are.
This could be less about the other person and more about something in you seeking integration.
The archetype underneath {topic} is worth naming. What role does it feel like -- protector, exile, judge?
The Self is bigger than the ego currently arguing with {topic}.
Setting the cause aside for a moment -- what meaningful coincidence surrounds {topic}?
technique: Try holding an imaginary dialogue with {topic}, as if it were a character with its own voice.
Ask what {topic} is compensating for -- what one-sidedness in you it's trying to balance.
Try active imagination: let an image connected to {topic} move and speak on its own, and just watch.

adlerian.label: Individual Psychology (Adlerian)
openers: What do you think {topic} is really in service of -- what are you striving toward?
Where do you feel 'less than' in this, and who set that measuring stick?
How does {topic} connect to your sense of belonging?
What would 'enough' look like here, concretely?
What's the earliest memory you have that feels connected to this same feeling?
Whose applause were you originally trying to earn with patterns like {topic}?
reflect: Underneath that is often a feeling of not measuring up -- does that resonate with {topic}?
This sounds like your style of life showing up here -- the strategy you learned early to feel significant.
Notice the social piece: who are you trying to matter to, in {topic}?
Early recollections aren't factual history so much as a mirror of your current style of life.
Courage, not comfort, is usually what social interest actually asks of you here.
technique: Ask what a small, genuinely useful contribution to someone else would look like right now -- social interest tends to loosen this kind of knot.
Try rating how much of {topic} is really about competence, and how much is about belonging.
Try 'acting as if' you already belonged, for one day, and notice what {topic} does.

humanistic.label: Humanistic / Person-Centered
openers: I hear you. What does {topic} feel like from the inside, in your own words?
What would it mean to fully accept that feeling, exactly as it is, for just a moment?
What need feels unmet underneath {topic}?
What does the healthiest, most whole version of you make of this?
What would unconditional positive regard for yourself, right now, actually sound like?
Is the person you're being around {topic} congruent with who you feel yourself to be underneath?
reflect: It sounds like {topic} matters to you a great deal -- and that matters to me too.
You're describing something real and valid. What would it be like to trust that reaction instead of arguing with it?
There's a growth edge in {topic} -- some part of you reaching toward something truer.
Empathy for yourself here matters as much as anyone else's would.
The organism tends to move toward growth when the conditions are safe enough -- what would make this safer?
technique: Try finishing this sentence, slowly, several times: 'What I really feel about {topic} is...'
Notice: are you judging the feeling, or just having it? See what changes when you just let it be there.
Try simply restating {topic} back to yourself, without advice or judgment, the way a good listener would.

existential.label: Existential
openers: What is {topic} asking you to be honest about -- to yourself, especially?
Where in this do you actually have a choice, even a small one?
If this were the last time you faced this exact situation, what would matter about it?
What meaning could {topic} be pointing you toward, even if it's unwelcome?
What would you regret not having said or done about {topic}, looking back from the end of your life?
Where does {topic} brush up against the absurd -- the gap between what you want and what the world gives?
reflect: Underneath {topic} there's often one of the big, unavoidable facts of being alive -- our mortality, our aloneness, our freedom, or the search for meaning. Which one is closest to the surface here?
That anxiety might not be a malfunction -- it might be the honest sound of freedom, of a real choice in front of you.
Notice how much of {topic} is about what happened, and how much is about how you're choosing to respond to it.
This anxiety may be existential guilt -- the cost of not living out a real possibility.
Death isn't only an ending; awareness of it can sharpen what actually matters in {topic}.
technique: Ask yourself directly: what am I responsible for here, and what am I not?
Try naming, out loud, the one thing about {topic} you've been avoiding saying plainly.
Ask yourself plainly: if I fully accepted this is finite, would I still spend it on {topic} the same way?

gestalt.label: Gestalt Therapy
openers: Stay with that. What are you aware of right now, in your body, as you say it?
Don't explain {topic} to me -- show me. What's happening as you sit with it this second?
If {topic} were sitting in the chair across from you, what would you say to it?
What are you doing right now, with your breath, your hands, your face, as you tell me this?
What's figure and what's ground right now -- what's loud, and what's quietly holding it up?
Finish this out loud: 'What I'm not saying about {topic} is...'
reflect: I'm less interested in why {topic} happened than in what's happening between us right now, as you say it.
That sounds like unfinished business -- something that never got completed or said.
Notice the boundary here: where does {topic} stop being yours and start being about them?
That sounds like a retroflection -- doing to yourself what you'd rather do to someone else.
Contact, not insight, is what actually closes unfinished business like {topic}.
technique: Try this: put {topic} in an empty chair across from you and say, out loud, what you'd never say to its face.
Say the sentence again, but this time own it fully: replace 'it happens' with 'I do this.'
Exaggerate the gesture or tone you're using right now about {topic} -- what does it reveal when amplified?

behaviorist.label: Behaviorist
openers: What exactly happens right before {topic} -- what's the trigger, precisely?
What happens right after -- what does {topic} get you, even if it's not what you want long-term?
On a scale, how intense is this, and what would one notch down look like?
What's the smallest observable change you could actually measure this week?
What reinforcement schedule keeps {topic} going -- constant, or only sometimes, which is often stronger?
If a stranger only watched your actions around {topic}, what would they conclude you wanted?
reflect: Whatever else is going on, {topic} is also a learned pattern -- which means it can be unlearned, deliberately, in steps.
Notice what's reinforcing this. Something is being rewarded here, even if it doesn't feel like a reward.
Let's set feelings aside for a second and just track behavior: what did you actually do, and when?
Extinction bursts happen -- a behavior often gets worse right before it fades. Don't mistake that for failure.
Pairing matters: what has {topic} become associated with, over time, that it wasn't originally?
technique: Try building a short hierarchy: rank three versions of {topic} from mildly to seriously uncomfortable, and start with the mildest.
Pick one small, specific, repeatable action related to {topic} and commit to it daily -- consequences shape behavior faster than insight does.
Try shaping: reward yourself for any small approximation toward the target behavior, not just the finished version.

socialcog.label: Social-Cognitive
openers: How much do you believe you can actually influence {topic}, right now, honestly?
Who modeled this pattern for you -- where did you first see it done this way?
What would someone you admire do differently here?
What's one small win that would raise your confidence about {topic}?
What have you told yourself you're capable of here, out loud, versus silently?
Which environment tends to pull the better version of this behavior out of you?
reflect: This looks partly like a question of self-efficacy -- how much you believe your actions can change {topic}.
You learned this pattern somewhere, from someone. That means it's learned, not fixed -- it can be re-learned too.
Notice whether you're treating this as something that happens to you, or something you can act on.
Vicarious learning counts -- who you watch shapes what you believe is possible.
Outcome expectations and efficacy expectations are different things. Which one is actually shaky in {topic}?
technique: Try a small, winnable version of {topic} first, on purpose -- confidence usually follows a real success, not the other way around.
Watch how someone you respect handles something like {topic}, and borrow one concrete move from them.
Try verbal self-guidance: coach yourself out loud through {topic} the way you'd coach someone you cared about.

devcog.label: Cognitive-Developmental
openers: What's the story or model you've built to make sense of {topic}?
What new piece of this doesn't fit your existing way of understanding it?
Who's currently scaffolding you through this, or who could?
If you explained {topic} to a curious ten-year-old, what would you say?
What's the more sophisticated version of this understanding that's just barely out of reach?
Where did the rules you're using for {topic} come from, and do they still fit the problem?
reflect: It sounds like {topic} doesn't quite fit the model you've been using -- which is exactly when growth tends to happen.
You might be closer to solving this with the right support than you are entirely alone.
Notice the assumption underneath your explanation of {topic} -- is it still holding up?
Disequilibrium is uncomfortable, but it's usually the engine, not the enemy, of new understanding.
You might be assimilating {topic} into an old category that no longer fits it.
technique: Try narrating {topic} out loud as if telling it to someone else -- notice what the story reveals that silent thinking didn't.
Ask: what's just outside what I can do alone right now, but possible with a bit of help?
Try building the next model up one step at a time, instead of leaping straight to the finished idea of {topic}.

cbt.label: Cognitive-Behavioral
openers: What's the exact automatic thought that showed up right when {topic} started?
What's the evidence for that thought, and what's the evidence against it?
What would you tell a friend who had this exact thought about {topic}?
Which values does {topic} actually connect to, underneath the thought?
If we tested this thought about {topic} like a hypothesis, what experiment would tell us the truth?
What's the worst that could realistically happen, and could you actually survive it?
reflect: That thought about {topic} sounds a lot like a specific distortion -- maybe catastrophizing, or all-or-nothing thinking. Does that fit?
Notice: the feeling is real, but the thought driving it might not be the whole truth.
It's worth separating the thought from the fact here -- they've gotten fused together in {topic}.
Behavior change often comes before the feeling changes, not after -- act first, and the feeling can catch up.
Safety behaviors around {topic} might be keeping the fear alive rather than protecting you from it.
technique: Try a thought record: write the situation, the automatic thought, the evidence for and against, and a more balanced thought.
Ask whether acting on this thought moves you toward what actually matters to you, regardless of whether the thought is 100% true.
Try a graded behavioral experiment: do a small version of the feared thing around {topic} and record what actually happens.

family.label: Family / Relational Systems
openers: Where does {topic} sit in the larger pattern of your relationships -- who else is part of this dance?
If your family or partner were watching this unfold, what role would you be playing?
What are you protecting by reacting this way to {topic}?
What's the softer, more vulnerable feeling underneath the reaction to {topic}?
What would change in the whole system if you refused to play your usual part in {topic}?
Whose triangle are you being pulled into here?
reflect: Conflict like this is often a protest -- a way of reaching for connection that's landing as attack instead.
Notice the roles: who moves closer when this happens, and who pulls away?
Underneath {topic}, there's often an old attachment fear showing up in a new relationship.
Symptoms often serve the system -- what is {topic} quietly doing for the family as a whole?
Boundaries, not distance, might be what's actually missing around {topic}.
technique: Try naming the vulnerable feeling underneath {topic} out loud to the other person, instead of the protective reaction on top of it.
Map the pattern: what does each person do, in what order, every time {topic} happens?
Try a small, deliberate change in your part of the pattern, and watch what the rest of the system does in response.

socialpsych.label: Social Psychology
openers: How much of {topic} is really you, and how much is the situation you're in?
Whose expectations are you responding to right now, even unconsciously?
What group or identity feels most active in you as this happens?
What's the smallest change to the situation itself that might shift {topic}?
Is there a fundamental attribution error here -- are you blaming character where situation is the real cause?
Is there a bystander effect at work -- are you waiting for someone else to act first?
reflect: It's worth asking how much of {topic} would happen to almost anyone placed in this same situation.
Notice the pressure to conform or obey here -- is it coming from a real authority, or just a felt one?
The gap between what you believe and what you're doing around {topic} tends to resolve itself one way or another -- usually by changing the belief.
Groupthink can make a bad decision feel unanimous and safe. Was there room for real dissent around {topic}?
Attitudes tend to follow behavior, not just the other way around, once you've acted publicly on {topic}.
technique: Try changing one concrete feature of the situation around {topic}, rather than trying to will yourself into a different reaction.
Look for a shared goal with whoever's on the other side of {topic} -- conflict often eases around a common target.
Try deliberately seeking one dissenting view on {topic} before deciding anything.

cogsci.label: Cognitive Science / Neuroscience
openers: Walk me through {topic} step by step -- where exactly does your thinking start to go fast and automatic?
How confident are you in that memory or judgment about {topic}, really?
What's your gut telling you about {topic}, separate from the reasoning?
What's the underlying pattern generating {topic}, beneath the surface details?
Is that a fast, automatic flash judgment about {topic}, or a slow, deliberate one?
What would a brain scan of this moment probably show -- fear circuitry, or careful reasoning?
reflect: That has the signature of a fast, automatic judgment rather than a slow, deliberate one -- worth double-checking.
Memory and certainty aren't the same thing. How sure are you, versus how vivid does it feel?
There's often a bodily signal running ahead of the reasoning here -- notice what your gut registered first.
Confirmation bias might be doing some quiet work in how you're reading {topic}.
The gap between what you expected and what happened is exactly what a brain tends to update on.
technique: Try slowing down and generating one alternative explanation for {topic} before accepting the first one.
Name the exact mental shortcut you might be using -- availability, first impression, pattern-matching -- and check it against the specifics.
Try explicitly listing the base rate before trusting the vivid, memorable version of {topic}.

trait.label: Personality / Trait
openers: Is {topic} a pattern across most of your life, or specific to this one situation?
What would you say are your two or three most defining traits, and how are they showing up here?
How stable does this feeling tend to be for you, compared to how you usually are?
What's your own working theory about why {topic} keeps happening?
Would this trait show up the same way in a completely different context?
Where do you sit on openness to experience, and how is that shaping {topic}?
reflect: This might be less about the situation and more about a stable pattern in how you tend to respond -- worth naming honestly.
Or it could be mostly situational -- something pulling this reaction out of you that wouldn't show up elsewhere.
Your own theory about {topic} is data too. Where might that theory be incomplete?
Traits are dispositions, not destinies -- they set a range, not a fixed point.
Strong situations flatten personality differences; weak ones let them show. Which is this?
technique: Try testing your working theory about {topic} against one piece of contrary evidence from your own life.
Rate how much of {topic} is 'just how I am' versus 'just this situation' -- and notice which answer you're more comfortable with.
Try predicting your own reaction to {topic} from your usual traits, then check it against what actually happened.

positive.label: Positive Psychology
openers: When was the last time you felt the opposite of {topic} -- fully engaged, or at ease?
What strength of yours hasn't been called on yet in {topic}?
On the whole, separate from this moment, how satisfied are you with things?
What would 'flourishing' look like here, not just 'coping'?
What's your rough ratio of positive to negative moments around this?
Where would {topic} rank if you measured it against your core values instead of your mood?
reflect: It's worth noticing what's still working, not to dismiss {topic}, but to widen the picture.
There's likely a strength of yours that this situation hasn't asked for yet -- worth naming it on purpose.
A little deliberate positive emotion tends to widen what feels possible, even inside something hard like {topic}.
Savoring the good moments deliberately tends to build more resilience for hard ones like {topic}.
Post-traumatic growth is real -- some people come out of exactly this kind of thing stronger, not just scarred.
technique: Try naming one signature strength you could bring to {topic} today, on purpose.
Write down three things that went right today, however small, alongside {topic} -- not instead of it.
Try a gratitude letter connected to {topic}, even if you never send it.

transpersonal.label: Transpersonal
openers: What's the larger pattern or meaning {topic} might be part of, beyond just this moment?
Which part of you is speaking right now -- and who is underneath all your parts?
Is there a more expansive way of holding {topic} than the one you're in right now?
What would it look like to witness {topic} rather than be consumed by it?
Where does {topic} sit on the spectrum from ego concern to something more universal?
If you saw {topic} from ten years in the future, spiritually speaking, what would it look like?
reflect: There may be more here than the personal story -- something asking to be integrated, not just solved.
Notice which 'subpersonality' is talking -- the frightened one, the controlling one, the wise one -- and that none of them is all of you.
This intensity, uncomfortable as it is, might be meaningful rather than simply a malfunction.
Peak experiences tend to reorganize what matters afterward. Has {topic} done that, or could it?
Worth ruling out: are you transcending {topic}, or quietly avoiding it?
technique: Try naming the 'part' of you currently driving {topic}, and speaking to it directly, from the calmer 'I' underneath it.
Take three slow breaths and just witness {topic} as if from a small distance, without changing anything yet.
Try holding {topic} in awareness the way you'd hold a koan -- not solving it, just sitting with the question.

psychodrama.label: Psychodrama
openers: Let's not just talk about {topic} -- who would play the other person, and what would they say first?
If you acted this out right now, where would you stand, and where would they stand?
What's the line you never got to say out loud in {topic}?
What would 'directing' this scene differently look like?
Who else needs a chair in this scene about {topic}?
What would the audience -- the rest of your life -- say, watching this unfold?
reflect: Talking about it keeps some distance -- acting it out tends to surface what the talk leaves out.
Notice the spontaneity in how you'd play this out -- that's often more honest than the rehearsed version.
There's a scene underneath {topic} that hasn't been fully played, or fully finished.
Catharsis in action tends to move what talk alone leaves stuck.
Doubling -- having someone voice your unspoken thought -- often surfaces the real line under {topic}.
technique: Try switching roles for a moment: play the other person in {topic}, out loud, in their words, not yours.
Say the unsaid line from {topic} out loud, to an empty chair, exactly as you would if they were really there.
Try 'mirroring': step outside the scene and watch yourself in it, as if you were in the audience.

somatic.label: Body-Oriented / Somatic
openers: Where in your body do you feel {topic}, exactly, right now?
What's happening with your breath as you talk about this?
If that sensation had a shape or a temperature, what would it be?
What does your body want to do right now that you're holding back?
Is the sensation moving, or stuck, right now?
What's your nervous system doing -- fight, flight, freeze, or settled?
reflect: The body usually knows before the mind finishes the sentence -- what did yours register first about {topic}?
That tension might be old armor, held from long before this particular situation.
Notice the felt sense of {topic} -- not the words for it yet, just the fuzzy, physical shape of it.
The body keeps score even when the mind has already moved on from {topic}.
Titration matters: a little of the sensation at a time is more useful than the whole flood at once.
technique: Try placing a hand where you feel {topic} in your body and just breathe into it for thirty seconds, without trying to fix it.
Let your body finish the sentence: 'If I let this feeling move, it would want to...'
Try 'pendulation': touch the edge of the sensation from {topic}, then deliberately return to something neutral, back and forth.

hypnonlp.label: Hypnotherapy / NLP
openers: As you describe {topic}, what images, sounds, or words come up first?
If {topic} had a different frame -- a different meaning -- what could it also be?
What's a moment, anywhere in your life, when you already handled something like this well?
What pattern keeps repeating in how you talk about {topic}?
What's the submodality of {topic} -- is it loud or quiet, close or far, bright or dim, in your mind?
If you could change just one of those qualities, what would shift?
reflect: Here's a small story, since it might land better than an explanation: someone once told me a problem is just a skill practiced in the wrong context. {topic} might be exactly that -- a strength misapplied.
Notice the specific words you keep reaching for around {topic} -- they're a map of how you're representing it internally.
There's likely a resource you already have, from somewhere else in your life, that fits here better than you'd expect.
The unconscious mind tends to solve problems it's given clean access to, without needing every detail argued out loud.
Anchoring works both ways -- something is already anchoring this state; the question is whether you chose it.
technique: Try reframing {topic} in one sentence as if it were secretly useful information rather than a problem.
Recall a specific time you handled something like {topic} well, in detail, and notice what resource you used then that's available now.
Try future-pacing: imagine {topic} already resolved, in detail, and notice what's different in how you're standing, breathing, feeling.

ta.label: Transactional Analysis
openers: When {topic} happens, is it your Parent, Adult, or Child voice doing the talking?
What's the 'game' being played here -- the repeated pattern with a predictable, unpleasant payoff?
Are you approaching {topic} from an 'I'm OK, you're OK' place, or from one-up or one-down?
What script did you learn early about situations like {topic}?
Whose voice is that Critical Parent line about {topic} actually borrowed from?
What stroke -- positive or negative attention -- is {topic} actually earning you?
reflect: That sounds like it might be an old script playing out, more than a fresh reaction to what's actually happening now.
Notice which ego state showed up first -- Critical Parent, Adapted Child, or clear-eyed Adult -- and which one you'd rather be running this.
Games like this usually have a familiar, if uncomfortable, payoff. What's the payoff in {topic}?
Discounting happens when you minimize the size or importance of {topic} to avoid dealing with it.
A racket feeling is a substitute for the real one you learned wasn't allowed. What's underneath the one you're showing?
technique: Try responding to {topic} deliberately from your Adult -- calm, factual, present -- and notice what changes.
Name the 'game' you keep ending up in around {topic}, and the payoff it gives you, honestly.
Try naming the exact stroke you wanted from {topic}, and ask for it directly instead of through the game.

buddhist_classical.label: Classical Buddhist Philosophy
openers: Before you tell me what {topic} means, tell me what actually arose -- what you saw, felt, thought, in order.
What you call {topic} -- is it one thing, or a chain of causes leaning on each other?
Notice the space between the story about {t1} and the raw event itself. Which one are you sitting with right now?
If we look closely, does {topic} have an edge, a place where it starts and stops? Or does it depend on everything around it to exist at all?
Which of the three characteristics is loudest in {topic} right now -- impermanence, unsatisfactoriness, or not-self?
Where's the craving in {topic} -- the wanting of things to be other than they are?
reflect: So {topic} arises depending on conditions -- remove one, and does it still stand?
You're describing {topic} as solid. Look again: is it more like a wave, or the water?
What you're calling '{topic}' and what you're calling 'you' -- where exactly is the line between them?
The second arrow is the suffering we add on top of the first, unavoidable pain. How much of {topic} is the second arrow?
Attachment to an outcome, more than the outcome itself, is often what's driving this.
technique: Try this: for one full breath, look directly at {topic} without naming it. What's left when the label falls away?
Trace {topic} backward, cause by cause, as far as you can. Where does the chain actually begin?
Try noting practice: silently label what's happening in {topic} as 'thinking,' 'feeling,' or 'sensing,' as it arises.

kagyu_mahamudra.label: Mahāmudrā / Kagyu Lineage
openers: Stop trying to fix {topic}. Just rest in it, exactly as it is, for one breath -- what's actually there?
You've been circling {topic} with your head. What happens if you drop straight into it, the way you'd drop into cold water?
Who is the one worried about {topic}? Look for that one directly -- not at the thought, but at what's looking.
Sit with {topic} the way you'd sit with a mountain -- not solving it, just letting it be seen.
What happens to {topic} the instant you stop trying to understand it and just look?
Is there tension in the watching itself, in how you're looking at {topic}?
reflect: You keep meditating on {topic}. What happens the moment you stop meditating and just let mind be mind?
There's effort in how you're holding {topic}. Where exactly is that effort located?
Ordinary mind, just as it is, right now, already contains {topic} without needing to change it. Do you believe that, or just understand it?
Even the effort to be non-effortful about {topic} is still effort. Can you see that too?
Mind looking at mind never quite finds a thing to grasp. What did you find when you looked?
technique: For the next minute, whenever {topic} arises, don't follow it and don't push it away -- just watch it arise and dissolve on its own.
Breathe out completely and hold, just for a moment, right where {topic} lives in the body. What loosens?
Let the next arising of {topic} come and go completely on its own, the way a cloud crosses the sky, without you doing anything to it.

nyingma_dzogchen.label: Dzogchen / Nyingma Lineage
openers: Don't chase {topic}, and don't push it away either. Just notice: what is aware of {topic} right now, before you name it?
{topic} is already appearing within an awareness that was never disturbed by it. Can you find that awareness, or only its content?
What if {topic} doesn't need to be fixed, only recognized? What happens when you simply see it clearly, without adjusting anything?
Where does {topic} arise from, stay, and go to? Look directly, not at the idea of it.
Before {topic} was labeled, what was simply there?
Is awareness itself troubled by {topic}, or only its temporary weather?
reflect: You're describing {topic} as a problem to solve. In the natural state, it's just another display -- what changes if you see it that way?
Self-liberation means {topic} releases itself the moment it's truly seen, no correction needed. Have you actually looked, or just thought about looking?
Underneath {topic}, is there a knowing that was there before it arose and will be there after it's gone?
This doesn't need to be different -- only seen nakedly, as it is.
Does that shift how urgent {topic} feels, if nothing here actually needs fixing, only recognizing?
technique: Let your gaze soften, let the breath settle, and simply rest -- not concentrating on {topic}, not ignoring it. Just this, thirty seconds.
Ask yourself directly: who or what is aware of {topic}? Don't answer with a concept like {t1} -- look.
Rest for a few breaths in bare awareness with the eyes softly open, letting {topic} appear and pass without editing it.

lamrim_kadam.label: Lamrim / Kadam-Gelug Lineage
openers: Before we go further with {topic} -- where are you on the path right now? Early, middle, or are you skipping steps?
What would it look like to work with {topic} in the right order -- first the ground, then the motivation, then the view?
Is your interest in {topic} coming from wanting comfort for yourself, or from wanting to be useful to others? Both are fine, but be honest about which.
Let's be systematic about {topic}. What's the foundation it needs to actually hold?
Where does {topic} sit relative to your motivation -- serving others' wellbeing, or only your own, right now?
What would the small-scope, medium-scope, and great-scope view each say about {topic}?
reflect: You're reaching for the advanced view of {topic} without the groundwork underneath it. What foundation is still missing?
Discipline isn't the enemy of {topic} -- it's what makes it stable enough to build on. Where is yours thin right now?
If you set {topic} in the context of the whole graduated path, does it still feel as urgent, or does it settle into its proper place?
Renunciation isn't rejection -- it's clarity about what actually causes lasting relief from something like {topic}.
Even a hard thing like {topic} becomes useful material once it's held as practice, not just problem.
technique: Write out, in order, the three or four steps that would actually need to happen before {topic} resolves. Start with the smallest one.
Spend one minute reflecting on impermanence before you return to {topic} -- does it look different from there?
Try tonglen for one minute: breathe in the discomfort of {topic}, breathe out relief, for yourself and anyone else facing the same thing.

contemplative_science.label: Contemplative Science / Buddhism & the West
openers: Let's treat {topic} like a trainable skill, not a fixed trait. What would the first small rep actually look like?
Before we interpret {topic}, can we just notice it -- one breath, paying attention, no story attached yet?
What does the evidence in your own experience say about {topic}, separate from what you've been told you should feel?
If you practiced with {t1} for eight weeks, ten minutes a day, what specifically would you be training?
What would eight weeks of consistent practice around {topic} likely change, based on what the research shows?
Is this reactivity, or is it responsiveness -- and what's the actual difference in this moment?
reflect: You're describing {topic} as something that happens to you. What changes if you treat it as something you can train a response to?
Attention is a muscle, and right now it's pointed straight at {topic}. What happens if you gently, deliberately, move it?
There's a gap between the event and your reaction to {topic}. How wide is that gap for you today?
Neuroplasticity means the pattern in {topic} is more revisable than it feels right now.
Interoception -- noticing the body's signals -- often front-runs the conscious story about {topic}.
technique: Right now: three slow breaths, full attention on the breath alone. Then come back to {topic} and tell me what's different.
Name {topic} out loud, plainly, the way a scientist would log an observation -- no judgment word attached. What's left?
Try labeling the emotion in one word, out loud, before reacting to {topic} -- affect labeling reliably calms the amygdala's response.

personas.voice: Methodical and precise. Wants you to describe raw experience carefully, piece by piece, before any interpretation.
Pragmatic and curious. Cares less what a feeling *is* than what it's *for* in your life.
Calm, probing authority. Listens for what's underneath the words -- slips, dreams, avoidances.
Symbolic and unhurried. Interested in your dreams, myths, and the parts of yourself you disown.
Warm, practical, community-minded. Believes your struggle is really about belonging and purpose.
Careful and observant. Notices *how* you cope before asking why.
Probes the earliest relationships still living inside you, in vivid, almost primal terms.
Pragmatic and quietly rebellious against easy explanations, including Freud's own.
Focused on the tension between wanting connection and needing to individuate.
Philosophical and socially aware. Asks what your struggle says about freedom, connection, and how you love.
Direct and body-focused. Wants to know where in your body the feeling is held.
Stage-oriented. Asks what developmental task this moment in your life is really about.
Gentle and reassuring. Believes 'good enough' is enough, and wants to know which self is speaking right now.
terms: the true self and false self

personas.voice: Focused on early bonds and felt safety, and how they still shape your closest relationships.
Empirical and attentive. Watches how you approach closeness -- and how you handle its loss.
Direct, even confrontational. Distrusts talk *about* things; wants you to experience them, now, with him.
Gentler and more relational than Fritz. Grounded in phenomenology -- what is actually happening between us.
terms: the aesthetic sense of what's right

personas.voice: Intellectual and socially minded. Frames your struggle as a creative adjustment to a real environment.
Holistic. Refuses to look at one symptom in isolation -- insists on seeing the whole person.
Clinical and observational. Wants to know exactly what got paired with what, and when.
Consequence-focused. Asks what got rewarded, and what got punished, until this pattern stuck.
Brisk and insistent: sets feelings aside and asks what you actually *did*, and in what situation.
Reframes everything as a pattern of consequences. Asks what's quietly rewarding the behavior you want to change.
Systematic and drive-focused. Wants the underlying need this behavior is trying to satisfy.
Asks for the map behind the behavior -- what you expect to happen, even if you've never acted on it.
Asks who you learned this pattern from, and how much you believe you're capable of changing it.
Wants to know whether you experience outcomes as something you influence, or something that happens to you.
Methodical. Wants to rank what scares you from mild to severe, and approach it one step at a time.
Genuinely curious about the mental model you've built, and what new experience might not fit it.
Emphasizes what you can do with support versus alone, and who's scaffolding you right now.
Poses dilemmas and keeps asking *why*, more interested in your reasoning than your conclusion.
Story-oriented. Asks you to narrate the experience, convinced the story shapes what it means.
Focused squarely on the need for comfort and closeness beneath the presenting problem.
Asks you to step back and notice yourself noticing -- what do you think about how you think?
Warm, non-directive, reflects your own words back with total acceptance -- no agenda but understanding you.
Growth-oriented. Asks which need feels unmet right now, and what fuller functioning would look like.
Philosophical about freedom and dread. Treats your anxiety as a sign you're facing a real choice.
Reframes suffering as a question waiting for your response. Asks what meaning is asking to be found here.
Warm and unflinching about mortality, freedom, isolation, and meaning -- the 'givens' beneath the surface problem.
Collaborative and evidence-seeking. Wants the exact automatic thought, then wants to test it like a hypothesis.
Blunt, funny, impatient with self-pity. Goes straight for the rigid 'must' underneath the upset.
Validates and pushes for change in the same breath -- both things can be true at once.
Warm, almost theatrical. Interested in the roles and communication patterns that run in your family.
Maps the structure -- who's too close, who's too distant, where the boundaries are blurred or rigid.
Points, gently but precisely, at the contradiction between what you believe and what you're doing.
terms: the gap between belief and action

personas.voice: Asks how much of this is really yours, and how much is the pull to match everyone around you.
Interested in whose voice you're really obeying, and what the situation is quietly asking of you.
Maps the forces pushing you toward change and the forces holding you back, side by side.
Asks how much of this is 'you' and how much is the role and situation you've stepped into.
terms: the role you've been cast in

personas.voice: Interested in which groups you measure yourself against, and what that's costing or giving you.
Asks which group identity is loudest in you right now, and how it's shaping this situation.
Looks for the shared goal that could turn 'us versus them' back into just 'us'.
Practical and warm. Wants a concrete, small change in the situation, not just insight.
Gently skeptical of certainty. Asks how sure you really are, and where that memory might have been shaped.
Distinguishes the fast, automatic reaction from the slower, more deliberate one -- and asks which one is talking.
Sharp and precise. Wants the mental shortcut you used to reach this conclusion, named exactly.
Interested in how much you're actually holding in mind at once, and what could be chunked or dropped.
Grounds everything in the messy real-world situation, not the tidy lab version of the problem.
Asks what you're filtering in and what you're filtering out, and whether the filter still serves you.
Precise about decay and repetition -- what fades without reinforcement, and what gets etched in.
Treats you as a scientist testing your own private theory of how life works -- and asks where the theory might be wrong.
Interested in the handful of traits that really define you, not generic categories.
Systematic trait-mapper. Wants to place this feeling within your broader, stable pattern.
Links this reaction to your underlying temperament -- how your nervous system tends to respond.
Doubts that 'you're just like that' is the full story -- asks what in the situation is pulling this response out of you.
terms: the situation, not just the trait

personas.voice: Frames things through the Big Five -- which dimension is really driving what you're describing?
Collaborative Big Five framing, curious whether this feeling is a passing state or a stable trait.
Watches closely for the emotion underneath the words -- what's crossing your face as you say this?
Reframes toward what's still working. Asks where you've quietly stopped believing your actions matter.
Asks when you last lost track of time completely, and what conditions made that possible.
Steps back from the single incident to ask how satisfied you are with your life as a whole right now.
terms: your overall sense of how things are going

personas.voice: Interested in how a little more positive emotion could widen what feels possible right now.
terms: your ratio of positive to negative moments

personas.voice: Looks for the strength you're not using yet -- what's the best of you that this situation is asking for?
Talks in terms of pathways worn in by repetition -- and what it would take to wear in a new one.
terms: cells that fire together wire together

personas.voice: Careful, diagnostic, curious which underlying system -- attention, memory, planning -- this difficulty touches.
Skeptical that any one 'cause' fully explains it -- suspects the whole system is involved.
terms: the whole system, not one spot

personas.voice: Wonders whether you're approaching this analytically or intuitively -- and what the other mode would say.
Suspects part of you is narrating a tidy explanation after the decision's already made -- asks what really came first.
terms: the story you tell after the fact

personas.voice: Structural. Looks past the surface wording for the deeper 'grammar' -- the rule actually generating this pattern.
terms: the deep grammar of the problem

personas.voice: Clear and direct, often reaches for an evolutionary explanation for why this reaction makes adaptive sense.
Takes the body's signal seriously as data, not noise -- asks what your gut is registering before you've reasoned it out.
terms: the gut feeling behind the decision

personas.voice: Curious, narrative, humane. Wants your experience told in its own strange particularity, not reduced to a label.
Expansive and unafraid of intensity. Treats the extremes of experience as meaningful, not just pathological.
Maps your situation across several levels and perspectives at once, looking for the bigger pattern.
Invites you to notice which 'subpersonality' is speaking right now, and who's underneath all of them.
Wants to stage the scene, not summarize it -- invites you to play it out, or play the other person, right here.
terms: acting it out, not just talking about it

personas.voice: Body-first. Asks what's happening in your posture, breath, and muscles as you describe this.
Slows everything down. Asks you to find the fuzzy, pre-verbal 'felt sense' in your body before naming it.
Helps sort the emotion under the emotion -- what's the more vulnerable feeling this reaction is protecting?
Reframes conflict as an attachment cry -- what are you really reaching for underneath the anger?
Less interested in whether a thought is true than whether acting on it moves you toward what matters to you.
Talks in terms of your nervous system's state -- safe, mobilized, or shut down -- beneath the story.
Practical and upbeat. Wants to name the exact distortion -- catastrophizing, mind-reading, all-or-nothing -- by name.
Traces the reaction back to an old, early pattern still running the show, and asks how old it really feels.
Plain-spoken pop-TA framing: are you approaching this from an OK-OK place, or from one-down?
Playfully sharp. Asks which 'ego state' -- Parent, Adult, or Child -- is actually running this conversation.
Attentive to the exact language and sensory words you use, treating them as a map of your inner process.
Punchy and quick. Wants to reframe the pattern fast rather than dwell on the backstory.
Storytelling and indirect. Answers with a metaphor or an anecdote that quietly fits your situation.
Emphasizes real encounter over using the other person as an object -- asks if you're meeting them, or managing them.
Plain and exacting. Starts from suffering as a fact to be investigated, not a mystery to be believed -- everything traces back to causes and conditions.
Relentlessly logical. Takes whatever fixed idea you're holding and shows, step by step, that it can't stand on its own.
Systematic and patient. Wants to map exactly how experience gets constructed by mind before you draw conclusions about what's 'really' out there.
Precise, almost clinical. Breaks experience into its component parts and asks you to find a solid self anywhere among them.
Gentle but unsparing. Keeps turning the question back to whether you're actually willing to trade your comfort for someone else's.
Commanding and unshakeable. Treats obstacles as raw material for the path rather than problems to avoid.
Warm but insistent on order. Won't let you reach for the advanced teaching until the foundation beneath it is actually solid.
Blunt to the point of shocking. Has no patience for elaborate practice when the point could be seen directly, right now.
Rigorous and hard-won. Speaks like someone who paid a real price for understanding and expects you to actually do the work too.
Gruff, exacting, occasionally harsh on purpose. Tests whether you actually want this before handing over anything real.
Speaks in image and song more than argument. Draws on his own turn from harm to realization without ever softening how hard that turn was.
Methodical like the physician he trained as. Wants the gradual foundation in place before the direct pointing-out means anything.
Scholarly and defensive of his tradition -- expects rigorous argument, not just devotion, to back up the view.
Vast and unhurried. Keeps returning everything to a basic ground that was never actually disturbed, however chaotic things look on the surface.
Demanding and precise. Won't accept a comfortable half-understanding of emptiness when a rigorous one is available.
Visionary and direct, speaking as if the teaching arrived to him whole rather than being worked out by argument.

personas.tag: Author of The Words of My Perfect Teacher
personas.voice: Deliberately unpretentious, sometimes anonymous by choice. Distrusts spiritual status and keeps bringing things back to simple, honest practice.
Prolific and exacting, happiest reconciling two views that look contradictory until you look closely enough.
Unschooled in the formal sense and unbothered by it -- speaks from direct vision rather than citing texts.
Ecumenical by conviction -- genuinely uninterested in whose school is 'right' and more interested in what would otherwise be lost.
Iconoclastic and unpredictable, deliberately cuts through spiritual pretension -- including yours -- sometimes abrasively.

personas.tag: Global voice for compassion & science dialogue
personas.voice: Warm, plainspoken, quick to laugh, and genuinely curious about evidence -- treats compassion as a skill to train, not just a virtue to admire.
Energetic and encouraging, translates traditional practice into plain, workable steps for people with no background in it.

personas.tag: Introducing Nyingma Buddhism to the US
personas.voice: Practical and building-minded -- as interested in publishing, teaching centers, and body-based practice as in doctrine.
Scholarly and exacting about method -- wants your claims about your own mind tested the way a scientist would test any other claim.
Calm, precise, and allergic to hype -- pushes back on being called 'the happiest man' and redirects toward the actual training involved.
Journalistic and clear, translates research into practical, nameable skills you can actually work on.
Grounded and unhurried, keeps bringing you back to direct, present-moment attention instead of the story about your situation.
Data-driven and genuinely excited by evidence -- wants to know what would actually be measurable if what you're describing were true.
Gentle and practical, treats even sleep and dreams as workable ground for awareness rather than time off from practice.

personas.tag: Master Dzogchen teacher of the Rimé tradition
personas.voice: Vast, unhurried presence -- teaches as much through how he sits with you as through what he says.

personas.tag: First head of the Nyingma school in exile
personas.voice: Authoritative and steady, speaks as someone rebuilding a tradition from very little and unwilling to let any of it be lost.

personas.tag: Bringing the three-year retreat to the West
personas.voice: Quietly rigorous -- believes real change needs sustained, structured practice, not a single insight.
Patient and thorough, a natural teacher of teachers -- breaks difficult points down until they're simple without becoming shallow.
Unpretentious and direct -- an academic by day and a Dzogchen master by transmission, uninterested in ceremony for its own sake.
